studies.title: A Meal For Three Strangers
studies.meaning: The reward is described before the reason, and then the reason turns out to be small and specific. A drink, a spring the drinkers themselves open. Then three lines of description: they keep vows, they fear a day whose harm spreads wide, and they give food away. Scholars differ over the phrase attached to the food, reading it as giving despite loving the food itself, or as giving out of love for God, and both readings are old.
studies.historicalContext: Classified as Medinan in the tradition this collection follows, though several classical authorities call it Meccan. Reports connect these ayat to a household that gave away its food on three successive nights, and the accounts of who was involved differ in the sources. What the wording itself establishes is the setting: a society in which captives were fed by the households that held them.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning wide open land, and behind the words for goodness and for dutifulness to parents. It names generosity of character rather than correctness, which suits a passage about giving food.

An intensive verb for splitting ground so water bursts out. The drinkers are given the action, so the spring is described as opened by them rather than found, which is unusual in a description of paradise.
From the root for a bird taking off. It describes harm that scatters in every direction rather than harm that is large, which is a different kind of fear.
A prisoner taken in conflict, from a root meaning to bind. Listing him third, after the poor and the orphan, extends the feeding to someone who was recently an enemy.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Captives in seventh-century Arabia were housed with families rather than in prisons, and the household fed them from its own pot. That put an enemy at the same meal in a year when food might be short. The three people named in this ayah, a poor man, an orphan and a captive, are the three categories with no claim on anyone: no earnings, no father, no tribe present to speak for them.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for what the cup is mixed with occurs only once in the Quran, here, and it names a cool, aromatic substance used in the region for scent and for preserving. Two ayat later the same passage names the reason for the reward, and it is a bowl of food handed to three people. The distance between the two descriptions is deliberate.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets an enormous reward beside a very small act and does not apologise for the disproportion. That is the point being made about how God deals with people. It also chooses its recipients carefully: the three named have nothing to give back and no power to repay, so the act described cannot be an investment in a relationship. And the vow kept in the line before makes the portrait one of promises honoured when nobody could enforce them.

crossReferences.why: Gives the words of the people described here, refusing both payment and gratitude in advance.
Names the same act as the steep road, and specifies the day on which it costs something.
Uses the same construction about giving what you love, in a longer list of what righteousness is.

studies.applyIt: Give away food this week rather than money, and give it to someone who cannot thank you usefully. Cook something extra, or hand a meal to a person you will not see again. The ayah names food specifically, and food has a quality money does not: you had to want it yourself for the giving to register.

studies.title: No Payment, No Thanks
studies.meaning: Their words are quoted, and the striking thing is what they refuse. Not payment only, but thanks, which is the currency generosity usually runs on. Then the account of what follows uses three verbs of God's doing: He guarded them, He met them with brightness and gladness, and He repaid them. What He repays is named as their patience rather than their giving, so the endurance behind the act is what is credited.
studies.historicalContext: Classified as Medinan in the tradition this collection follows, though the classical authorities differ. Reports attach the passage to a household that gave away its food, and they vary in detail. What the sentence itself preserves is a piece of speech: the words a giver says to a recipient, which is a rare thing for the Quran to record from an ordinary person rather than from a prophet.

keyTerms.note: An idiom for doing something for God alone, using the word for a face. The tradition takes it as naming the direction of an act rather than a part of God, and the whole phrase means for His sake.

Refusing this is the sharper half of the sentence. Payment can be declined without cost, but declining a recipient's gratitude removes the last thing a giver usually keeps, which is being known to have given.
A rare five-letter word describing a face contracted with strain, paired here with a word for scowling. Arabic builds longer words for heavier meanings, and this is among the longest in the Quran.
The word for the bloom on a plant with enough water, used of a face that looks well. It answers the drawn, contracted face of the day they feared, feature for feature.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Giving in Arabia was rarely private. A generous man was named in poetry, and the naming was part of the transaction; hospitality bought standing as much as it fed anyone. Refusing thanks in that culture was not modesty, it was opting out of the entire system by which giving was rewarded. The sentence quoted here would have sounded strange to the person receiving the food.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran almost always quotes prophets, angels, or opponents. Here it quotes two sentences from unnamed believers speaking to a poor man at their door, and preserves them exactly. It is one of a very small number of places where ordinary people's words are recorded as scripture, and what they say is a refusal rather than a prayer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Sincerity is defined here by subtraction. The passage does not describe an inner state; it lists what the givers declined to take, and the list ends with the one thing almost nobody declines. That makes sincerity checkable in principle: it shows up in what you refuse rather than in what you feel. The reward is then attached to patience, which quietly says that the refusing was the difficult part.

crossReferences.why: Names the failure this speech avoids, a gift undone afterwards by being mentioned to the person who received it.
Describes the same motive in the same words, adding that no one has any claim on him being repaid.
Gives the act these words accompany, food handed to a poor man, an orphan and a captive.

studies.applyIt: Do one good thing this week and take active steps to keep it unknown. Not just refrain from mentioning it; arrange it so nobody can trace it back to you. Then notice the small pull to leave a clue. That pull is what the sentence in this ayah is declining, and it is easier to see once you have felt it.
